latin.2603: XXI. Qui in Belgio Remonstrantes dicuntur, sive Arminiani, maxime probant & arcte retinent gratiae distinctionem in sufficientem atque efficacem, eamque putant multis scripturae locis subnixam, & necessariam plane ad justitiam divinam tuendam. Proinde negant gratiam sufficientem aliam non esse, quam quae est efficax, hoc est, quam quae actu ipso hominem conversum dat. Licet enim, inquiunt; maxima sit gratiae sufficientis ad operandum in homine conversionem efficacia & ἐνέργεια, tamen non semper illa, vitio nempe & culpa hominis, habet effectum, ipsumque conversionis ἀποτέλεσμα. Ut videre est in eorum Synodo in declaratione sententiae Remonstrantium circa tertium & quartum articulum pag. 15.
latin.2604: XXII. Quae sit autem ratio sufficientis istius gratiae, distinctius explicant in declarationis jam dictae initio, thesi sexta. Quanquam, inquiunt, pro liberrima Dei voluntate, maxima sit gratiae divinae disparitas; tamen Spiritus Sanctus tantum gratiae omnibus & singulis, quibus verbum praedicatur, confert, aut conferre paratus est, quantum ad promovendam suis gradibus hominum conversionem sufficit: eoque gratia sufficiens ad fidem & conversionem non tantum iis obtingit, quos, juxta decretum absolutae Electionis, salvare velle dicitur Deus; verum etiam iis, qui actu ipso non convertuntur.
latin.2605: XXIII. Caeterum efficaciam gratiae positam nolunt in omnipotente quadam agendi vi, & voluntatis ad bonum inevitabili determinatione; aut etiam in vocationis congruitate, ut Scholastici quidam. Sed in tali gratiae operatione quae effectum suum certissime sortitur, quum novam illi contumaciam, & rebellionem homo non opponit, quam ex se opponere potuisset. Quae sunt eorum verba eadem pagina 15. citatae declarationis.
latin.2606: XXIV. Pagina vero sequenti ut actus gratiae divinae sigillatim exponant, observant tria in homine corrupto egere correctione & regeneratione, mentem, voluntatem, affectum, ac triplici huic subjecto gratiae divinae triplices actus accommodant. Primum ergo, ut ipsi sententiam suam exprimunt, Mentem Deus verbo & spiritus sui illuminatione de voluntate sua salutifera certiorem reddit, eamque ut assentiatur verbi veritati facit. Et quanquam homo possit vel per negligentiam, vel per malitiam voluntatis, hanc illuminationem & revelationem, tunc cum ea primitus vel externe, vel etiam interne menti fit, respuere, contemnere, nec eam alte in animum admittere, unde ignorantia affectata oritur; fieri tamen non potest ut si quando veritas clare & perspicue a Spiritu Sancto menti praesentetur, intellectus non assentiatur, aut judicium suspendat, sed ab objecto ita proposito, & a spiritu insinuato, determinatur ad assentiendum, nec potest intellectus ex se illi illuminationi resistere, cum ab objecto suo determinetur.
latin.2607: XXV. Voluntatem insuper Deus in obsequium suum flectit, & ad actus fidei & obedientiae ita inclinat per Spiritum suum sanctum verbo utentem, ut voluntas per illam operationem non solum possit obedire, sed & per illam operationem obediat quoties obedit; non ex se, aut per se, aut a se.
latin.2608: XXVI. Addunt & hoc ad exaggerandam omnimodo gratiam, etiam supernaturalem potentiam voluntati conferri, & hac ratione Deum immediate in voluntatem agere, modo illa actio voluntatem non necessitet antecedenter, & libertatem potentiamque non volendi tollat.
latin.2609: XXVII. Deinde subjungunt mente illuminata, & voluntati concessa supernaturali potentia, partim per illuminationem, partim per virium immediatam infusionem, Deum quoque affectus nostros, & partem illam sensitivam corrigere, & bonis desideriis, quorum objecta monstrat intellectus, actus vero imperat voluntas, afficere; quibus affectibus magis, magisque correctis, castigatis, & in ordinem redactis, promptior & facilior, ac minus impedita postmodum redditur voluntas ad exercendos pietatis actus, non usque adeo, uti ante, reluctantibus affectibus, & lege illa in membris belligerante.
latin.2610: XXVIII. Caeterum ut exponant quae sint in hac gratiae efficacia & operatione tum verbi Dei, tum Spiritus Sancti verbo utentis partes, dicunt verbum suadere, sed spiritum verbo utentem persuadere: ac praeterea tutius semper esse statuere, actionem spiritus, qua in voluntatem agit, sibi subordinatam habere actionem verbi, quam si actionem spiritus faciamus collateralem actioni verbi in voluntatem, & juxta verbum operari dicamus, non per verbum, ne Enthusiastis doctrinae suae principia, & nescio quos arcanos motus, tractiones, impulsus, quos facile quisque sibi imaginari potest, largiri videamur.
latin.2611: XXIX. Verum ut clarius adhuc mentem suam explicent circa gratiae Divinae vim & efficaciam, multas quaestiones movent, ad quas breviter & distincte respondent. Si quaeratur ex nobis, inquiunt, An Dei convertentis actio tantum moralis sit suadendo, proponendo, invitando? Respondemus plusquam moralem esse, & si excitantem spectemus gratiam, dicimus in ipsam voluntatem quoque potentiam supernaturalem infundi distinctam ab illuminatione; si vero cooperantem, dicimus eam, Physicam vocari posse, & realem ac propriam habere efficientiam.
latin.2612: XXX. Si quaeratur, An nulla sit spiritus actio immediata in voluntatem? non diffitemur eam dari. Si quaeratur, An idem sit modus operandi quoad efficaciam gratiae in vivificatione intellectus, affectus & voluntatis? Respondemus non esse, sed modum agendi in voluntatem esse resistibilem. Nec tamen videntur simpliciter negare per gratiam quosdam motus irresistibiliter in voluntate produci, sed juxta eorum hypotheses, hoc videtur restringendum ad efficaciam illam, per quam voluntas simpliciter ex mala, bona redditur.
latin.2613: XXXI. Si quaeratur, An praeter mentis illustrationem, & affectuum excitationem, & voluntatis invitationem nihil faciat Gratia per modum principii, vel antecedenter ad conversionem? Respondemus facere. Quod autem gratia praeterea facit, videtur, ex eorum mente, esse novarum illarum virium infusio, de qua antea locuti sunt.
latin.2614: XXXII. Si quaeratur an positis omnibus operationibus quibus ad conversionem in hominibus efficiendam Deus utitur, conversio saepe vel nunquam non sequatur? Respondemus, posita gratia antecedente & praeveniente saepe non sequi, posita cooperante nunquam non.
latin.2615: XXXIII. Si quaeratur An conversio contingens & incerta sit, An vero necessitate causae aut eventus infallibiliter sequatur in eo qui convertitur? Respondemus conversionem esse contingentem quia libera est; nec tamen Deo incertam, quia praecognita est; nec sequi necessitate causae, sive consequentis, quia resistere poterat homo, sed necessitate consequentiae, sive ratione praescientiae infallibiliter sequi, in eo quem conversum iri praescivit Deus.
latin.2616: XXXIV. Si quaeratur, Quae causa sit cur hic convertatur, ille non? Respondemus, hic convertitur, quia Deus hunc non opponentem novam contumaciam convertit; ille non convertitur, quia novam contumaciam opponit. Quaeres, cur hic opponit novam contumaciam, alter non? Respondemus, hic opponit quia opponere vult; ille non opponit quia a gratia movetur ne opponere velit. Quaeres, Annon ille qui non opponit novam contumaciam, & per consequens convertitur, majorem habeat gratiam, quam qui opponit, & per consequens non convertitur: Respondemus antecedentem & praevenientem gratiam aequalem esse posse: sed cooperantem habet prior, non posterior.
latin.2617: XXXV. Porro ex his manifestum est Remonstrantes, secundum propria principia, facile conciliare posse arbitrii libertatem cum gratiae efficacia: quandoquidem supponunt gratiam quae voluntatem movet ad conversionem, agere modo resistibili, hoc est, tali ut voluntas gratiae cedere possit, & operationem illius suscipere, & rursus etiam possit gratiae obicem ponere, & operationem illius impedire. Quod his verbis exponunt ipsi declarationis saepius allegatae pagina decima septima. Huic autem suae conversioni, ad quam scilicet a gratia movetur, homo ex insita sibi pravitate, & in res mundanas affectu, obicem ac impedimentum liberum ponere potest, & ponit saepe, sive voluntas praedicationem Evangelii externam negligat, & susque deque habeat, tum quum ejus audiendi copia sit homini: aut auditum verbum perfunctorie tractet magis rebus mundanis intentus: aut alio modo impediat, quominus ipsi doctrinae Evangelicae veritas, necessitas, utilitas a Spiritu Sancto persuadeatur; sive verbo quidem ejusque veritati assentiatur, sed voluntatem secundum verbi istius praescriptum componere, eique obedire non velit: & laxatis carni habenis spiritum extinguat, spiritui resistat, & bona desideria cogitationesque saepius coelitus infusas & oblatas volens elidat & exterminet. Quare dicimus hominis voluntatem ad volendum bonum non necessitari, sed hominem posse ex se resistere, hoc est, non velle, & saepe actu non velle, & resistere gratiae sufficientis operationibus.

sections.title: The Remonstrants keep the division of grace
sections.pass_a: XXI. Those who in the Low Countries are called Remonstrants, or Arminians, most strongly approve & firmly retain the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious, and think it supported by many places of scripture, & plainly necessary for upholding divine justice. Accordingly they deny that sufficient grace is none other, than that which is efficacious, that is, than that which in very act gives man converted. For although, they say; the efficacy & energeia of sufficient grace for working conversion in man be very great, yet it does not always, namely by the vice & fault of man, have its effect, and the very apotelesma of conversion. As may be seen in their Synod in the declaration of the opinion of the Remonstrants on the third & fourth article page 15.
pass_b: Thesis XXI. The Remonstrants of the Low Countries, also called Arminians, strongly approve the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious and hold firmly to it. They think it rests on many passages of Scripture and is plainly needed to defend God's justice.

So they deny that sufficient grace is only the grace that is efficacious, the grace that actually produces a converted person. 'Although,' they say, 'sufficient grace has the greatest efficacy and energy (energeia) for working conversion in a person, it does not always, through the person's own vice and fault, take effect and reach the actual outcome (apotelesma) of conversion.' This can be seen in their Synod, in the declaration of the Remonstrants' opinion on the third and fourth articles, page 15.

sections.title: Enough grace given to all who hear the word
sections.pass_a: XXII. But what the account of that sufficient grace is, they explain more distinctly at the beginning of the declaration just mentioned, in the sixth thesis. Although, they say, according to the most free will of God, there be the greatest disparity of divine grace; yet the Holy Spirit confers, or is ready to confer, so much grace on all & each, to whom the word is preached, as suffices to promote by its degrees the conversion of men: and so grace sufficient for faith & conversion befalls not only those, whom, according to the decree of absolute Election, God is said to will to save; but also those, who in very act are not converted.
pass_b: Thesis XXII. They explain more precisely what this sufficient grace consists in at the beginning of the same declaration, in the sixth thesis. 'Although,' they say, 'by God's entirely free will there is the widest inequality in divine grace, the Holy Spirit still gives, or stands ready to give, to each and every person to whom the word is preached as much grace as is enough to advance their conversion step by step.
So grace sufficient for faith and conversion comes not only to those whom God is said, under the decree of absolute election, to will to save, but also to those who are not in fact converted.'

sections.title: Where the Remonstrants place efficacy
sections.pass_a: XXIII. But they will not have the efficacy of grace placed in some omnipotent force of acting, & an inevitable determination of the will to good; or again in congruity of calling, as some Scholastics. But in such an operation of grace as most certainly obtains its effect, when man does not oppose to it new obstinacy, & rebellion, which of himself he could have opposed. Which are their words on the same page 15 of the cited declaration.
pass_b: Thesis XXIII. They refuse, however, to place the efficacy of grace in some all-powerful force of action and an unavoidable determination of the will to good, or, as some Scholastics do, in the congruity of the call.

They place it rather in an operation of grace that most surely achieves its effect whenever a person sets against it no new obstinacy and rebellion, which he could have set against it of himself. These are their words, on the same page 15 of the declaration cited.

sections.title: Grace acting on the mind
sections.pass_a: XXIV. But on the following page to set out the acts of divine grace one by one, they observe that three things in corrupt man need correction & regeneration, the mind, the will, the affection, and to this threefold subject they fit threefold acts of divine grace. First then, as they themselves express their opinion, God by his word & the illumination of his spirit makes the mind more certain of his saving will, and makes it assent to the truth of the word. And although man can either through negligence, or through malice of the will, reject, despise this illumination & revelation, at the time when it is first made to the mind either externally, or even internally, nor admit it deep into the soul, whence affected ignorance arises; yet it cannot happen that if at any time the truth be clearly & plainly presented to the mind by the Holy Spirit, the intellect should not assent, or suspend judgment, but by the object so proposed, & by the spirit insinuated, it is determined to assent, nor can the intellect of itself resist that illumination, since it is determined by its object.
pass_b: Thesis XXIV. On the following page, to set out the acts of divine grace one at a time, they note that three things in corrupt man need correcting and regenerating: the mind, the will and the affections. To this threefold subject they match three kinds of act of divine grace.

First, in their own words: 'By his word and the enlightening of his Spirit, God assures the mind of his saving will and brings it to assent to the truth of the word. Through carelessness or through malice of will, a person can spurn and scorn this enlightening and revelation when it first comes to the mind, outwardly or even inwardly, and can refuse to take it deep into his soul, and from this comes affected ignorance.

Even so, once the truth is set clearly and plainly before the mind by the Holy Spirit, the intellect cannot fail to assent or hold back its judgment. It is determined to assent by the object so presented and by the Spirit who instils it, and the intellect cannot of itself resist that enlightening, since its object determines it.'

sections.pass_a: XXV. God moreover bends the will to his obedience, & so inclines it to acts of faith & obedience through his holy Spirit using the word, that the will through that operation not only can obey, but also through that operation obeys as often as it obeys; not of itself, or through itself, or from itself.
pass_b: Thesis XXV. 'God also bends the will to obey him, and through his Holy Spirit, who uses the word, he so inclines it to acts of faith and obedience that through that working the will not only is able to obey but actually obeys, every time it obeys, through that same working, and not of itself, by itself or from itself.'

sections.title: Supernatural power given to the will
sections.pass_a: XXVI. They add this too to magnify grace in every way, that supernatural power also is conferred on the will, & in this way God acts immediately on the will, provided that action does not necessitate the will antecedently, & take away the liberty & power of not willing.
pass_b: Thesis XXVI. To magnify grace in every way they add that a supernatural power is also given to the will, and that in this way God acts directly on the will, so long as that action does not necessitate the will beforehand or remove its freedom and its power of not willing.

sections.title: Grace acting on the affections
sections.pass_a: XXVII. Then they subjoin that the mind having been illuminated, & supernatural power having been granted to the will, partly through illumination, partly through immediate infusion of strength, God also corrects our affections, & that sensitive part, & affects them with good desires, whose objects the intellect shows, but whose acts the will commands; which affections being more & more corrected, chastised, & reduced to order, the will is afterwards rendered more prompt & easy, and less hindered for exercising acts of piety, the affections not resisting so much, as before, & that law warring in the members.
pass_b: Thesis XXVII. They go on to say that once the mind has been enlightened and the will given supernatural power, partly by enlightening and partly by a direct infusion of strength, God also corrects our affections and that sensitive part of us. He moves them with good desires, whose objects the intellect points out and whose acts the will commands.

As those affections are corrected, disciplined and brought into order more and more, the will becomes readier, easier and less hindered in practising acts of devotion, since the affections and that law at war in our members no longer fight back as much as before.

sections.title: The word persuades through the Spirit, not beside it
sections.pass_a: XXVIII. But to set out what in this efficacy & operation of grace are the parts both of the word of God, and of the Holy Spirit using the word, they say that the word urges, but the spirit using the word persuades: and moreover that it is always safer to hold, that the action of the spirit, by which it acts on the will, has the action of the word subordinate to itself, than if we make the action of the spirit collateral with the action of the word on the will, & say that it works beside the word, not through the word, lest we seem to grant to the Enthusiasts the principles of their doctrine, & I know not what secret motions, drawings, impulses, which anyone can easily imagine for himself.
pass_b: Thesis XXVIII. To show what parts the word of God and the Holy Spirit who uses the word each play in this efficacy and working of grace, they say that the word urges but the Spirit using the word persuades.

They add that it is always safer to hold that the Spirit's action on the will has the word's action under it, than to make the Spirit's action run alongside the word's action on the will and say that he works beside the word rather than through it. This is so that we do not seem to hand the Enthusiasts the principles of their teaching, and who knows what hidden motions, drawings and impulses, which anyone can easily imagine for himself.

sections.title: Is God's converting action only moral?
sections.pass_a: XXIX. But to explain their mind still more clearly about the force & efficacy of Divine grace, they raise many questions, to which they answer briefly & distinctly. If it is asked of us, they say, Whether the action of God converting be only moral by urging, proposing, inviting? We answer that it is more than moral, & if we regard exciting grace, we say that into the will itself also a supernatural power is infused distinct from illumination; but if cooperating, we say that it, can be called Physical, & has real and proper efficiency.
pass_b: Thesis XXIX. To make their mind on the force and efficacy of divine grace clearer still, they raise many questions and answer them briefly and precisely. 'If we are asked,' they say, 'whether God's converting action is only moral, working by urging, setting before, inviting, we answer that it is more than moral.

If we look at stirring grace, we say that a supernatural power, distinct from enlightening, is poured into the will itself as well; if at cooperating grace, we say that it can be called physical and has a real and proper efficiency.'

sections.title: Immediate action on the will, but resistible
sections.pass_a: XXX. If it is asked, Whether there is no immediate action of the spirit on the will? we do not deny that it is given. If it is asked, Whether the mode of operating as regards the efficacy of grace is the same in the vivifying of the intellect, the affection & the will? We answer that it is not, but that the mode of acting on the will is resistible. Yet they do not seem simply to deny that some motions are produced irresistibly in the will by grace, but according to their hypotheses, this seems to be restricted to that efficacy, by which the will simply from bad, is made good.
pass_b: Thesis XXX. 'If it is asked whether the Spirit has no direct action on the will, we do not deny that there is one. If it is asked whether grace works with the same kind of efficacy in quickening the intellect, the affections and the will, we answer that it does not: its way of acting on the will is resistible.'

They do not, however, seem to deny outright that grace produces some motions in the will irresistibly. On their assumptions this seems to be limited to the efficacy by which the will is made, without qualification, good from bad.

sections.title: When conversion follows grace
sections.pass_a: XXXII. If it is asked whether all the operations being posited which God uses for effecting conversion in men, conversion often or never fails to follow? We answer, antecedent & prevenient grace being posited it often does not follow, cooperating being posited never not.

'If it is asked whether, when God has put in place every working he uses to bring about conversion in people, conversion often fails to follow or never fails, we answer: with antecedent and prevenient grace in place, it often does not follow; with cooperating grace in place, it never fails to follow.'

sections.title: Conversion contingent, yet infallibly foreknown
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. If it is asked Whether conversion is contingent & uncertain, Or whether it follows infallibly by necessity of cause or of event in him who is converted? We answer that conversion is contingent because it is free; yet not uncertain to God, because it is foreknown; nor does it follow by necessity of the cause, or of the consequent, because man could resist, but by necessity of the consequence, or by reason of foreknowledge it follows infallibly, in him whom God foreknew would be converted.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIII. Their next question is whether conversion is a contingent and uncertain thing, or whether, in the person converted, it comes about infallibly through a necessity of cause or of outcome. Their answer: 'Being free, conversion is contingent; being known to God in advance, it is not uncertain to him.

Its necessity is not that of the cause, or of the consequent, for the person was able to resist. Its necessity is that of the consequence, or of foreknowledge, and in that way it comes about without fail in anyone God foreknew would be converted.'

lemmas.latin: Respondemus conversionem esse contingentem quia libera est
lemmas.gloss: we answer that conversion is contingent because it is free

lemmas.latin: nec tamen Deo incertam, quia praecognita est
lemmas.gloss: yet not uncertain to God, because it is foreknown

lemmas.latin: sed necessitate consequentiae, sive ratione praescientiae infallibiliter sequi

choices.why: Scholastic distinction: necessity of the consequent (the thing itself is necessary) against necessity of the consequence (only the inference holds, here from foreknowledge).

sections.title: Why one is converted and another not
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. If it is asked, What is the cause why this one is converted, that one not? We answer, this one is converted, because God converts him not opposing new obstinacy; that one is not converted, because he opposes new obstinacy. You will ask, why does this one oppose new obstinacy, the other not? We answer, this one opposes because he wills to oppose; that one does not oppose because he is moved by grace not to will to oppose. You will ask, Has not he who does not oppose new obstinacy, & consequently is converted, greater grace, than he who opposes, & consequently is not converted: We answer that antecedent & prevenient grace can be equal: but the former has cooperating, not the latter.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIV. 'If it is asked why this person is converted and that one not, we answer: this one is converted because God converts him while he sets up no new obstinacy; that one is not converted because he sets up new obstinacy. You will ask why this one sets up new obstinacy and the other does not. We answer: this one sets it up because he wants to; that one does not, because grace moves him not to want to.

You will ask whether the one who sets up no new obstinacy, and so is converted, does not have greater grace than the one who sets it up, and so is not converted. We answer that their antecedent and prevenient grace can be equal, but the first has cooperating grace and the second does not.'

lemmas.latin: quia Deus hunc non opponentem novam contumaciam convertit
lemmas.gloss: because God converts him not opposing new obstinacy

sections.title: The Remonstrants reconcile freedom and efficacy easily
sections.pass_a: XXXV. Further from these things it is manifest that the Remonstrants, according to their own principles, can easily reconcile the liberty of choice with the efficacy of grace: since they suppose that the grace which moves the will to conversion, acts in a resistible manner, that is, such that the will can yield to grace, & receive its operation, & again also can put an obstacle to grace, & hinder its operation. Which they themselves set out in these words on the seventeenth page of the declaration often alleged. But to this his conversion, to which namely he is moved by grace, man from the depravity implanted in him, & his affection to worldly things, can put a free obstacle and impediment, & often puts it, whether the will neglects the external preaching of the Gospel, & makes light of it, at the time when the opportunity of hearing it is given to man: or treats the word heard perfunctorily being more intent on worldly things: or in some other way hinders, that the truth, necessity, utility of the Evangelical doctrine should be persuaded to it by the Holy Spirit; or assents indeed to the word and its truth, but will not compose the will according to the prescription of that word, and obey it: & the reins being slackened to the flesh quenches the spirit, resists the spirit, & willingly crushes & exterminates good desires and thoughts often infused & offered from heaven. Wherefore we say that the will of man is not necessitated to will good, but that man can of himself resist, that is, not will, & often in act not will, & resist the operations of sufficient grace.
pass_b: Thesis XXXV. It is clear from this that the Remonstrants, on their own principles, can easily reconcile freedom of choice with the efficacy of grace. They assume that the grace moving the will to conversion acts in a resistible manner: the will can give way to grace and accept its working, and can also block grace and hinder its working. They say so themselves on page 17 of the declaration so often cited:

'To this conversion of his, to which grace moves him, a person, from his inborn depravity and his attachment to worldly things, can freely set a barrier and hindrance, and often does. His will may neglect the outward preaching of the Gospel and treat it as of no account when he has the chance to hear it; or handle the word he has heard carelessly, being more taken up with worldly things; or in some other way prevent the Holy Spirit from persuading it of the truth, necessity and usefulness of the Gospel teaching.

Or he may assent to the word and its truth, yet refuse to shape his will by what that word prescribes and to obey it; and, giving the flesh free rein, he quenches the Spirit, resists the Spirit, and wilfully crushes and roots out good desires and thoughts often poured in and offered from heaven. So we say that the human will is not necessitated to will good, but that a person can resist of himself, that is, refuse to will, often actually refuse, and resist the workings of sufficient grace.'
